Score 80-100 for articles directly covering: news and events in Williams Lake, Quesnel, 100 Mile House, Bella Coola, Horsefly, Likely, Anahim Lake, Alexis Creek, or the Cariboo Regional District; local government and civic decisions (City of Williams Lake, City of Quesnel, CRD, District of 100 Mile House); local health services and emergency closures; local economy, businesses, and community programs; Cariboo arts, culture, and community events; AND digital equity, rural internet access (fiber, fixed wireless, Starlink), and connectivity serving these specific communities. Articles from local Cariboo news sources (mycariboonow.com, wltribune.com, quesnelobserver.com, 100milefreepress.net, cfjctoday.com) covering Cariboo community life should score 65-85. Score 50-79 for: BC provincial news directly affecting Cariboo communities, rural Canadian community stories closely paralleling Cariboo life, digital equity and rural internet broadly. Score 20-49 for: general BC news that may affect rural areas, broader rural Canada topics without specific Cariboo tie-in. Score 0-19 for: national/international news without Cariboo relevance, pure tech or entertainment with no community angle. Penalise heavily (score 0–20): international geopolitical and war news with no Cariboo tie-in; science discoveries without a local community connection; consumer tech reviews and gadget guides; wildlife and conservation stories not involving Cariboo communities or First Nations; BC provincial news without direct Cariboo-region relevance. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.content_html:

The Arctic sea ice melt season is roughly 40 days longer than it was in 1979, yet its rapid expansion unexpectedly leveled off around 2010. Scientists say changing clouds and increasingly thin ice may explain the pause, but continued Arctic warming could eventually trigger another period of rapid change.

items.title: [livescience.com] Swallowable paper battery powers medical devices in pigs
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers developed a small battery made from magnesium and molybdenum trioxide that can be swallowed to power temporary medical devices inside the gastrointestinal tract. In pig tests, the battery produced a peak voltage of 1.84 volts and operated for up to three days, powering a wireless throat tag that transmitted to a receiver 1.5 metres away and a capsule that electrically stimulated the stomach for 20 minutes [scimex.org#1][livescience.com#1]. The battery uses materials intended to break down in the body after use, potentially removing the need to retrieve conventional batteries from temporary ingestible devices. The study remains at an early animal-testing stage: researchers tested a small number of pigs, and the circuit board did not fully degrade but passed in the animals' feces [scimex.org#1]. MIT said the researchers built two versions—a 7.5-millimetre disc and a 24-millimetre rectangular bar—for possible drug-delivery, sensing and other applications [mit.edu#1].

items.title: [phys.org] Fire amoeba breaks complex-life heat tolerance record at 63°C
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Scientists have identified a new amoeba, Incendiamoeba cascadensis, that can eat, move and reproduce in water as hot as 63°C (145°F) at California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park, setting a record for the highest temperature known to support eukaryotic reproduction. The NASA-supported study, published in Cell on Sept. 22, found that the organism remains active at about 64°C and can recover after five minutes at 70°C, although exposure to 80°C proved fatal [phys.org#1][nasa.gov#1][livescience.com#1][sciencenews.org#1]. The finding challenges the previous 60°C upper limit for eukaryotic growth and reproduction, based on the heat sensitivity of proteins and other complex cellular structures. Researchers said the amoeba withstands the heat by changing shape and forming a protective outer layer; genetic analysis also identified genes associated with repairing heat-damaged proteins [nasa.gov#1][science.org#1][orf.at#1]. The work is relevant to astrobiology because scientists use extreme environments on Earth to assess where complex life might survive on Mars and other worlds [nasa.gov#1][npr.org#1].

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists say a critical Atlantic Ocean current is weakening and the effects could be global
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Scientists have found strong observational evidence that a key part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation has been weakening across a wide stretch of ocean for nearly two decades. The slowdown could eventually reshape weather patterns, rainfall, storms, winters, and coastal sea levels around the Atlantic.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

An extra 2.7 million lives could be saved in the next pandemic if countries share vaccines in a less selfish way, a new study has found – although the death toll in richer countries would rise.

Researchers modelling a hypothetical global outbreak of flu found that fast-tracking vaccine development could cut deaths from 58.5m to 23.9m.
